title: ⭐⭐ Revision: judging your work and helping a partner

questions.prompt: Chaima found the lesson easy and understood the whole of it. Which sentence does she use to say both of those things?

options.text: I found the lesson easy, but I understood only a little.
I found the lesson easy, and I understood everything.
I found the lesson boring, and I understood most of it.
I found the lesson fairly difficult, but I understood everything.

questions.explanation: Easy plus the whole lesson understood gives "I found the lesson easy, and I understood everything." "I found the lesson easy, but I understood only a little." judges the difficulty correctly but leaves her with very little understood, "I found the lesson fairly difficult, but I understood everything." makes the lesson hard, which is the opposite of easy, and "I found the lesson boring, and I understood most of it." answers about interest instead of difficulty and lowers the amount understood.

questions.prompt: Tarek suggested: "What about writing the difficult words on cards?" How does he say the same thing with "You could…"?

options.text: You could to write the difficult words on cards.
You could writing the difficult words on cards.
You could write the difficult words on cards.
You could writes the difficult words on cards.

questions.explanation: "You could write the difficult words on cards." is right: could is followed by the base verb alone. "You could to write the difficult words on cards." adds the to of the infinitive, which could never takes; "You could writing the difficult words on cards." keeps the -ing form that belongs after What about and not after could; and "You could writes the difficult words on cards." adds the present -s that a base form never carries.

questions.prompt: Mariem replies: "No, I wasn't." Which question is she answering?

options.text: Are you ready for the test?
Did you revise for the test?
Was the test difficult for you?
Were you ready for the test?

questions.explanation: A short answer answers with the helper of the question and speaks for the same person: asked about herself, the pupil replies with I, and the past of be follows that new subject — were with you becomes was with I. So "No, I wasn't." answers "Were you ready for the test?" "Are you ready for the test?" would be answered with No, I'm not, "Did you revise for the test?" with No, I didn't, and "Was the test difficult for you?" keeps the same past of be but has the test as its subject, which gives No, it wasn't.

questions.prompt: Firas was bored by the story from the first line to the last. Which sentence does he use to say so?

options.text: I found the story boring.
I found the story quite interesting.
I found the story very interesting.
I found the story too interesting.

questions.explanation: The scale runs from interesting through quite interesting down to boring, and the end that matches Firas is "I found the story boring." "I found the story quite interesting." says it held his attention a little, "I found the story very interesting." says it held it completely, and "I found the story too interesting." misuses too, which means more than I want and would turn a good point into a complaint.

questions.prompt: Three of these self-evaluation questions ask about a state or a quality. Which one asks about a finished action instead?

options.text: How interesting was the last lesson?
Which text was too long for you?
What is your main difficulty?
When did you read the second text?

questions.explanation: A finished action is asked about on the did line of the builder, WH word + did + subject + base verb, and "When did you read the second text?" is the only question built on it. "What is your main difficulty?", "Which text was too long for you?" and "How interesting was the last lesson?" all use a form of be, the line kept for a state or a quality.

questions.prompt: Hiba wants to tell her partner that planning the week brings more reading time, using the "If you…" structure. Which sentence is correct English?

options.text: If you will plan your week, you will find more time.
If you plan your week, you will find more time.
If you plan your week, you will finding more time.
If you will plan your week, you find more time.

questions.explanation: The if half stays in the present and will goes in the other half, so the sentence is "If you plan your week, you will find more time." "If you will plan your week, you will find more time." puts will after if, "If you will plan your week, you find more time." makes the same mistake and then drops will where it is needed, and "If you plan your week, you will finding more time." puts an -ing form after will instead of the base verb.
